title: Savoy Pioneers Celebrate Sixtieth Anniversary
text:
Savoy Pioneers Celebrate Sixtieth Anniversary

MRS. J. A. GLASS
Special to The Democrat

SAVOY, Texas.—Three Savoy pioneers will be at home to their friends June 5 when two of the group, Mr. and Mrs. Tom W. McSpadden, celebrate their sixtieth marriage anniversary. The third is Mrs. J. A. Glass of Savoy whose residence in this section has been as long as that of her brother and sister.

Mr. and Mrs. McSpadden were married June 5, 1872 in Texas. She was Miss Margaret Benton, born Nov. 22, 1850 in McMinn county, Tenn. She was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. F. Benton and was one of 10 children of a second marriage, there being four of the father's first marriage. Only two brothers and Mrs. McSpadden are living of the 14 children now.

TOM W. McSPADDEN

After their marriage, Mr. and Mrs. McSpadden lived on the Captain William Thompson farm a few years and then bought a farm just north of Savoy, which they still own. They saw the wild turkey and deer disappear with the longhorn cattle, and fertile fields develop from prairie. Six children came to their home. Four of them who are living are Sam McSpadden, Dallas, Mrs. Minnie Hodges, Mrs. Mamie Pritchett, Savoy and Will McSpadden, Denison.

The children return home often for a reunion. The home has modern conveniences, with a radio to add to the comfort. Both old people are active, though Mrs. McSpadden is a sufferer from rheumatism. Mr.

MRS. TOM W. McSPADDEN

McSpadden, however, has never in his life had a serious illness, is straight as an arrow and works every day. They are both members of the Methodist church.

Mr. McSpadden has one brother and three sisters living. One of the latter is Mrs. Glass, widow of the late Rev. J. A. Glass, Baptist minister. Mr. McSpadden is a native of Monroe county, Tenn. and was born Sept. 22, 1849, one of a family of eleven children. At the age of 21 he set out in the world for himself, came to Texas and settled where Savoy now is. At that time only three small shacks could be seen on the prairies. He began, like Abraham Lincoln, splitting rails and in a few months started farming, which was his life work.
